claim: Taxonomy of metric types: statistical/deterministic (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, Levenshtein, BERTScore), LLM-based (G-Eval, QAG, Prometheus), RAG metrics, DAG decision-tree.
quote: BLEU calculates the precision for each matching n-gram between an LLM output and expected output; ROUGE calculates recall; BERTScore computes the cosine similarity between the contextual embeddings; G-Eval first generates a series of evaluation steps using chain of thoughts (CoTs) before using the generated steps to determine the final score.

claim: Three eval categories crystallized in 2026: deterministic, rubric (LLM-judge or human), and composite; frameworks run offline, online and pre-merge.
quote: Three eval categories have crystallized: deterministic, rubric (LLM-judge or human), and composite. A modern eval framework runs at three lifecycle points: offline against curated datasets, online against live production traffic, and pre-merge in CI.

claim: A golden dataset is a curated, labeled ground-truth dataset used to evaluate LLMs.
quote: A golden dataset for LLM evaluation is a curated and labeled dataset used as ground truth to evaluate large language models.

claim: Self-preference bias is the tendency of LLMs to overestimate their own outputs; driven by perplexity, with GPT-4 scoring 0.520 on the bias metric.
quote: LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators, regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated. The paper reports a self-preference bias score of 0.520 for GPT-4.

claim: Frontier LLM judges fail 50%+ of bias tests; biases are default behaviors not edge cases.
quote: Position bias, verbosity bias, and self-preference bias are not theoretical risks disclosed in footnotes. They are default behaviors that silently distort quality scores in every pipeline that does not explicitly mitigate them.

claim: Verbosity bias inflates preference for longer answers by 15-30 points (Wang et al. 2023); self-preference adds 10-25% uniform bias.
quote: Wang et al. 2023 measured 15 to 30 points of inflated preference for verbose answers across GPT-4, Claude, and PaLM-2 judges. Self-preference adds 10 to 25 percent uniform bias.

claim: Strong LLM judges hit 80-90% agreement with humans (comparable to inter-annotator agreement); sample 5-10% of verdicts for human re-grade and monitor kappa drift.
quote: Strong LLM judges achieve 80-90% agreement with human evaluators on many quality dimensions, which is comparable to inter-annotator agreement between humans. Sample 5-10% of judge verdicts and have a human re-grade them, tracking agreement over time.

claim: Calibration loop: collect human corrections, build few-shot examples, track agreement over time; strong judges ~80% human agreement.
quote: Collect human corrections on evaluator judgments, use those corrections to build calibrating few-shot examples, and track agreement metrics over time to verify improvement. Strong LLM judges reach approximately 80% agreement with human evaluators.

claim: CLT-based uncertainty estimates fail below ~a few hundred samples, dramatically underestimating uncertainty; use Bayesian/bootstrap instead.
quote: CLT-based methods perform very poorly, usually dramatically underestimating uncertainty (i.e. producing error bars that are too small).

claim: Report SE of the mean; binary SE=sqrt(mu(1-mu)/n); use paired differences and clustered SE; detecting half the effect needs 4x samples.
quote: Report the standard error of the mean alongside the mean. Detecting a gap half the size requires 4x the number of samples. If questions are correlated, the standard error increases by 3x. Paired differences provide a free reduction in estimator variance.

claim: Position bias measured via Repetition Stability, Position Consistency, Preference Fairness; GPT-4/Claude-3.5 PC ~0.82, Claude-3-Haiku drops to 0.23 on DevBench; bias driven by quality gap not prompt length.
quote: Claude-3.5-Sonnet (0.82 MTBench), GPT-4 (0.82 MTBench); Claude-3-Haiku drops to 0.23 on DevBench. Position bias is strongly affected by the quality gap between solutions but very weakly correlated with the length of prompts.

claim: Rubric design: binary for hard gates, ordinal for gradations; 4-7 independent criteria with anchor examples; target Krippendorff alpha near 0.8; swap-and-average for position, cross-family judge for self-preference.
quote: Binary pass/fail is best for hard gates; ordinal scales are better when the thing being judged has legitimate gradations. Four to seven criteria, each tied to a failure mode the business actually cares about. Always use a judge from a different model family than the one being tested.

claim: Human-LLM alignment is highest on a 0-5 grading scale.
quote: Grading Scale Impact on LLM-as-a-Judge: Human-LLM Alignment Is Highest on 0-5 Grading Scale.

claim: Judges select the first response in ~68% of comparisons even when humans prefer the second; GPT-4 ~40% inconsistency under (A,B)/(B,A) swap.
quote: Judge models selecting the first response in 68% of comparisons, even when human annotators clearly prefer the second option. GPT-4 shows approximately 40% inconsistency when evaluated with both (A,B) and (B,A) orderings.

claim: LLM judge agrees with humans ~85% of the time, higher than two humans agree with each other.
quote: An LLM judge agrees with human reviewers about 85% of the time - higher than two humans agree with each other on the same task.

claim: DeepEval open-source LLM eval framework implementing G-Eval, RAG metrics, DAG.
quote: DeepEval is an open-source LLM evaluation framework.

claim: RAGAS reference-free RAG eval metrics: faithfulness, answer relevancy, contextual precision/recall.
quote: Ragas: supercharge your LLM application evaluations.

claim: lm-evaluation-harness, the de-facto benchmark runner for golden/static datasets.
quote: A framework for few-shot evaluation of language models.

claim: Five judge biases that silently kill evals and concrete fixes.
quote: The 5 Biases That Can Silently Kill Your LLM Evaluations (And How to Fix Them).

claim: Position bias persists in rubric-based (pointwise) judging, not only pairwise.
quote: Am I More Pointwise or Pairwise? Revealing Position Bias in Rubric-Based LLM-as-a-Judge.

claim: 2026 guide: reference-based metrics for constrained outputs, LLM-judge for open-ended, human eval for ground truth.
quote: Three methods measure performance: reference-based metrics for constrained outputs, LLM-as-a-judge for open-ended quality, and human evaluation to establish ground truth.

claim: Practitioner reference for statistics applied to LLM evals (CIs, significance tests).
quote: Statistics for LLM Evals.
